topic: diagnosing sign and denominator errors in conic equations

traps.desc: read the number inside the bracket as printed instead of flipping its sign

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response says the standard form is written with a subtraction, so a plus sign inside the bracket means the coordinate is negative -- the bracket has to be read as x minus negative five. Full credit refers to the subtraction built into the standard form; saying only that the sign is flipped, with no reason, is partial credit.

traps.desc: reported the right-hand side as the radius instead of taking its square root
assumed the denominator under the x term is always the larger one, without comparing the two

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response says the longer axis belongs to whichever denominator is larger, not to the x term by default -- here the larger denominator sits under the y term, so the major axis is vertical. Full credit states the compare-the-denominators rule and applies it to this equation; simply reporting the corrected number is not a diagnosis.

traps.desc: added the two denominators instead of subtracting, applying the hyperbola rule to an ellipse
subtracted the denominators as for an ellipse instead of adding
copied the linear coefficient straight across as the centre coordinate, without halving it or flipping its sign
copied the linear coefficient straight across as the centre coordinate

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response says each centre coordinate is half the linear coefficient with its sign reversed, because completing the square puts half of that coefficient inside the bracket and the standard form then subtracts it. Full credit names both moves, the halving and the sign reversal, since the quoted answer got both wrong.

traps.desc: inverted the ratio, putting the denominator of the negative term on top
took the square root of the constant term as the radius, without completing either square
halved the linear coefficient correctly but did not reverse its sign

problems.desc: Part (c): the first quoted answer treats the constant term as though it were already the square of the radius, skipping the two completing constants that have to be added to the other side; the second halves correctly but keeps the sign of the linear coefficient instead of reversing it. A correct response names both faults separately. Full credit distinguishes them; describing one error twice, or calling them both careless arithmetic, does not.
